It promotes tenfold's identity and access governance platform as a no-code solution for reviewing and revoking unnecessary shared-file access.
KEY POINTS
  • 01The article states that organizations using Microsoft 365 often lack visibility into who can access potentially sensitive files shared through Teams, OneDrive, and SharePoint.
  • 02It cites a Wire survey in which 61% of security leads said access to shared files often remains active longer than intended, while more than one-third reported difficulty identifying who can access sensitive shared files.
  • 03Microsoft 365's built-in reporting can show recent sharing-link activity or site-level lists of shared files and recipients, but the article says these options require substantial manual investigation.
  • 04The article argues that access reviews should involve the people who originally shared files, because they are best positioned to determine whether access is still needed.
  • 05The sponsored article promotes tenfold's shared-content governance tools for centralized reporting and owner-led reviews that can confirm or revoke access.

The sponsored article discusses the difficulty organizations face in tracking access to files shared through Microsoft 365 services such as Teams, OneDrive, and SharePoint. It says shared access can remain active after its original purpose ends, such as when a freelancer leaves a project but retains access to its SharePoint folder. The article cites a Wire survey in which 61% of security leads said shared-file access often lasts longer than intended, and more than one-third reported difficulty identifying who can access sensitive shared files.

According to the article, Microsoft 365 provides reports on recent sharing-link activity and site-level lists of shared files and their recipients, but these require extensive manual review and may lack useful context. It argues that the person who originally shared a file is best placed to decide whether access is still needed, making owner-led access reviews important. The article promotes tenfold’s shared-content governance tools, which it says provide centralized visibility across Teams, OneDrive, and SharePoint and allow file owners to confirm or revoke access through personalized review dashboards.

  • The article emphasizes that a high number of new sharing links is not inherently suspicious, because legitimate activities such as onboarding a supplier can produce the same signal.
  • It argues that access decisions are highly dependent on the original business purpose, making the person who shared a file the most appropriate reviewer of whether access should continue.
  • Site-level reports may provide detailed lists of shared files and recipients, but the article says their practical value is limited at enterprise scale because collecting and reviewing them across all SharePoint and OneDrive locations is time-consuming.
  • The article presents owner-facing, personalized review dashboards as a way to delegate access checks to non-IT staff while allowing them to confirm or remove access directly.

This sponsored article says that businesses using Microsoft 365 can lose track of who can open files shared through Teams, OneDrive, and SharePoint. For example, contractors or former project members may keep access after their work ends, potentially exposing sensitive company information. It promotes tenfold software as a way for organizations to see shared files in one place and ask file owners to confirm or remove access.

KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft Teams plans to let administrators customize the file extensions blocked by its Weaponizable File Protection feature.

Microsoft Teams plans to let administrators customize the file extensions blocked by its Weaponizable File Protection feature. The built-in safety feature scans Teams conversations and blocks chat or channel messages that contain dangerous, high-risk file attachments. Microsoft says the capability is in development and is scheduled to begin rolling out in November 2026.

Administrators will be able to use Microsoft’s recommended default blocked-file list or tailor it to their organization’s security requirements; currently, they cannot change the list. When generally available, the control will support Android, desktop, iOS, macOS, and web clients in standard multi-tenant cloud environments worldwide. The update is part of broader Teams security work that includes controls for external users, QR codes from external senders, suspicious guest invitations, and external bots in meetings.

  • Teams administrators currently cannot alter the default list of blocked file types, so the planned update changes a previously fixed security control into an organization-specific policy.
  • The new file-blocking control is intended to let organizations either retain Microsoft’s recommended defaults or adapt them to their own security requirements.
  • Microsoft’s recent Teams security changes address several entry points for social engineering, including file attachments, external users, QR codes, guest invitations, and meeting bots.
  • The feature is planned for all major Teams client platforms, meaning an organization’s file-blocking policy is intended to apply across desktop, web, and mobile use.

Microsoft Teams plans to let company administrators choose which types of attached files are blocked in chats and channels, starting in November 2026. The change affects organizations using Teams and gives them more control over stopping files that could carry harmful software. It matters because criminals, including ransomware groups, have used Teams messages and calls to trick employees, so stronger controls can help reduce the chance of a damaging compromise.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a specific upcoming Microsoft Teams security-control change with broad relevance for organizations that use Teams. It is not urgent or an active incident, but customizable attachment blocking can materially affect how administrators tailor collaboration security policies.

  • 01Check Point released security updates for CVE-2026-91843, a critical stack-based buffer overflow in the login process for Security Management Server instances.
  • 02The flaw also affects Check Point Log Server systems and can allow attackers without privileges to execute code remotely with root privileges without user interaction.

Check Point Software released security updates for CVE-2026-91843, a critical stack-based buffer overflow in the login process of Security Management Server instances. The flaw also affects the company’s Log Server, which collects and stores logs from Check Point firewalls. An attacker without privileges can exploit it in a low-complexity attack requiring no user interaction to execute code remotely with root privileges.

Check Point has not reported active exploitation of CVE-2026-91843, but says teams can look for “Administrator failed to log in: Username too long” alerts in Audit and Admin login logs. Customers unable to deploy the latest LivePatch can harden vulnerable systems and restrict SmartConsole access to trusted IP addresses or subnets. The article also notes that Check Point recently patched critical flaws CVE-2026-85102 and CVE-2026-85103, and the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre expects exploitation attempts against those two issues soon.

  • CVE-2026-91843 can be detected through a highly specific log indicator: an “Administrator failed to log in: Username too long” alert in Audit and Admin login logs.
  • Organizations that cannot immediately install the LivePatch have a concrete interim option: limit SmartConsole trusted-client access to known IP addresses or subnets.
  • Check Point stated that the separate CVE-2026-85103 flaw affects every Security Management Server deployment regardless of configuration, including environments where VPN is not enabled or configured.
  • Although CVE-2026-91843 is not known to be exploited, the article notes that other recent Check Point authentication-bypass zero-days were exploited and that Dutch authorities expect attempts against CVE-2026-85102 and CVE-2026-85103 soon.

Check Point released updates for a serious weakness that could let an outsider take full control of systems used to manage its network security equipment and store its security records. The issue affects all of the company’s Security Management Server setups and its Log Server, and it can be abused without an account or help from a user. This matters because a criminal who gains this level of control could interfere with an organization’s defenses, and Check Point has recently fixed several other serious flaws that security authorities expect attackers to target soon.

Microsoft fixes bug behind ‘Defender Antivirus is turned off’ alerts

Microsoft fixed a bug that falsely warned users that Defender Antivirus was turned off even though protection remained active. The fix is included in Microsoft Defender Antivirus version 4.18.26080.4, released September 17.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft fixed a bug that incorrectly reported Microsoft Defender Antivirus as turned off even when it was operating normally.
  • 02The fix was delivered in Microsoft Defender Antivirus version 4.18.26080.4, released on September 17.
  • 03The erroneous Windows Security notifications affected supported Windows client and server versions, including Windows 11 26H1 and Windows Server 2025.
  • 04The false alerts could appear at Windows startup and intermittently afterward, and persisted even when notification settings were disabled.
  • 05Microsoft had acknowledged the issue in late August after reports indicated it had affected Windows Insider Release Preview users since at least June.

Microsoft has fixed a known issue that incorrectly displayed alerts saying Microsoft Defender Antivirus was turned off after recent updates. The antivirus was still functioning correctly and its settings showed it as active. Microsoft said the fix is included in Microsoft Defender Antivirus update version 4.18.26080.4, released on September 17.

The false Windows Security alerts affected all supported Windows client and server versions, including Windows 11 26H1 and Windows Server 2025. They could appear when Windows started and intermittently afterward, and they persisted even when notifications were disabled. Microsoft acknowledged the issue in late August, while reports indicated that users in the Windows Insider Release Preview Channel had experienced it since at least June.

The article notes that Microsoft has previously asked users to disregard other incorrect Windows alerts after updates. These included erroneous BitLocker encryption warnings, invalid Windows Recovery Environment installation failures, Windows Firewall configuration alerts, and CertificateServicesClient errors. Microsoft also released emergency Windows updates this week to address Remote Desktop Services, Hyper-V, and USB audio problems caused by September 2026 security updates.

  • The warnings were not evidence that protection had stopped: Microsoft stated that Defender Antivirus continued functioning correctly and its settings remained active.
  • Disabling notifications did not prevent the false “turned off” alerts, making the issue more disruptive than a typical optional notification problem.
  • Although Microsoft publicly acknowledged the problem in late August, reports indicate that Release Preview Channel users had encountered it since at least June.
  • The issue extended beyond consumer PCs to supported Windows Server systems, including Windows Server 2025.

Microsoft fixed a problem that wrongly told people their built-in Windows virus protection was turned off, even though it was still working. The false warnings affected supported Windows computers and servers, including newer Windows 11 and Windows Server versions, and could appear at startup or later. This matters because misleading security warnings can worry users and make it harder to know when a real protection problem needs attention.

Fake LastPass Authenticator GitHub repos push new Rapuncel infostealer

SEO-optimized fake GitHub repositories impersonating LastPass and dozens of other brands are distributing the Rapuncel infostealer, which uses a Microsoft-signed kernel driver to disable security products. Users should download software only from official sources and avoid promoted or dubious search results.
KEY POINTS
  • 01An ongoing campaign uses search-optimized fake GitHub repositories impersonating LastPass and at least 39 other companies to distribute the previously undocumented Rapuncel information stealer.
  • 02Victims who click download buttons on the fake repositories are redirected to servers that provide ZIP files inflated to as much as 148 MB, containing a renamed Microsoft Visual Studio CoreCLR Debugger configured to load a malicious DLL.
  • 03The payload installs Rapuncel and a Microsoft-signed Alinubx.sys kernel driver disguised as an NVIDIA component, which is designed to terminate 145 antivirus and endpoint security processes.
  • 04Rapuncel steals credentials from 25 web browsers, data from 30 cryptocurrency wallets, session credentials for Discord, Steam, and Telegram, Windows Credential Manager contents, selected documents, screenshots, and system information.
  • 05The malware sends compressed stolen data to 2.26.126[.]50 over raw TCP and maintains persistence through a Windows service that can terminate reactivated security tools after reboot.

An ongoing campaign uses SEO-optimized GitHub repositories impersonating LastPass and at least 39 other companies to distribute a previously undocumented information stealer called Rapuncel. Victims searching for LastPass Authenticator or other software may follow links to fake repositories, where download buttons redirect them to payload servers. The servers deliver ZIP archives inflated to as much as 148 MB, apparently to evade security scans.

The archives contain a renamed copy of Microsoft Visual Studio CoreCLR Debugger, vsdbg.exe, configured to sideload a malicious DLL that installs Rapuncel and the Alinubx.sys kernel driver. The Microsoft-signed driver is disguised as an NVIDIA component and is designed to terminate 145 antivirus and endpoint detection and response processes, including products protected by Protected Process Light. Rapuncel then steals browser credentials, cryptocurrency-wallet data, messaging and gaming session credentials, Windows Credential Manager contents, selected documents, screenshots, and system details before sending compressed data to an external endpoint. The malware also persists through a Windows service so it can terminate reactivated security tools after reboot.

  • The campaign uses a driver signed through Microsoft’s Windows Hardware Compatibility Publisher chain that is not currently on Microsoft’s vulnerable-driver blocklist, allowing it to terminate security products despite their protected-process safeguards.
  • Rather than using an obviously suspicious executable, the installer is a renamed legitimate Microsoft Visual Studio CoreCLR Debugger that loads a malicious DLL alongside it.
  • Rapuncel is designed to bypass Google’s app-bound browser-encryption protection by placing a helper component inside Chrome, Edge, and related browsers and using their own elevation service.
  • The malicious ZIP archives are deliberately enlarged to up to 148 MB, an apparent attempt to evade security scanning, while the malware’s Windows service lets it disable security tools again after a reboot.

Criminals are creating fake GitHub download pages that pretend to offer LastPass Authenticator and software from at least 39 other companies. People who find these pages through web searches may download a program that shuts off security software and steals saved browser passwords, cryptocurrency wallet data, chat and gaming account sessions, documents, screenshots, and computer details. This matters because the stolen information can expose personal accounts and financial assets, and the harmful program can keep running even after the computer restarts.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This reports an active malware-distribution campaign using fake GitHub repositories, a Microsoft-signed kernel driver to disable 145 security products, and a stealer targeting browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, and Windows credentials. The broad impersonation of LastPass and dozens of other brands makes it relevant to security teams and end users.

Gyazo server flaw exploited to steal 23.6 million user records

Gyazo suffered a server vulnerability breach that exposed roughly 23.6 million user records and metadata for 490 million images, potentially including credentials, session tokens, and private-image information. KEY POINTS
  • 01Gyazo said attackers exploited a server vulnerability on September 11, 2026, and accessed its database containing approximately 23.62 million user records.

  • 03Gyazo said 490 million image metadata records were exposed, mostly for images uploaded before January 2019, including image IDs, upload IP addresses, User-Agent strings, EXIF location data, OCR-extracted text, image titles, source URLs, and hashed passphrases for private images.

Gyazo said attackers exploited a server vulnerability on September 11, 2026, gaining unauthorized access to its database and stealing approximately 23.62 million user records. The company detected suspicious activity the following day and fixed the weakness, but said the data had already been taken. Gyazo temporarily suspended its service while it conducts maintenance and investigates the incident with external experts.

The exposed records may include names, email addresses, password hashes, user and device IDs, login session IDs, X integration tokens, Google SSO email addresses, profile information, subscription details, billing status, and usage statistics. Gyazo also said 490 million image metadata records were exposed, mostly tied to images uploaded before January 2019, including image IDs, upload IP addresses, location information, extracted text, titles, and source URLs. Because image IDs may enable access to associated content and attackers obtained a list of private images, Gyazo disabled access to affected files and cannot rule out that some private images were viewed.

  • The incident affects more than account records: exposed image IDs may be usable to reach associated files, prompting Gyazo to disable access to files linked to exposed records.
  • The exposed data includes both login session IDs and X integration tokens, which are distinct from passwords and increase the importance of reviewing account access after the breach.
  • Most of the 490 million exposed image metadata records relate to images uploaded before January 2019, indicating that older uploads are a major part of the exposure.
  • Gyazo cannot rule out that some private images were viewed because the attackers obtained a list identifying them, even though the company found no indication that data was deleted.
  • Gyazo said its investigation found no evidence that other Helpfeel or Cosense services had data stolen.

Gyazo, a service that stores and shares screenshots and recordings, says intruders used a weakness in its systems to copy about 23.6 million user records. The exposed information may include names, email addresses, protected password data, account login details, payment status, and details connected to hundreds of millions of uploaded images. Some private images may have been viewed, and the leaked image details could help someone find associated files, so Gyazo has temporarily blocked access to affected files. Users should change their Gyazo password and any other account passwords they reused.

Microsoft fixes broken copy and paste for Excel 2016 users

Microsoft released KB5002665 to fix a KB5002914 regression that caused copy, paste, autofill, and formula dragging to fail silently in MSI-based Office 2016. Users of other affected Excel versions must use Paste Special or consider rolling back the security update, which removes important vulnerability patches.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft said the September 2026 KB5002914 security update introduced a code regression that can cause Excel copy-and-paste operations, autofill, and formula dragging to fail silently.
  • 02Microsoft released KB5002665 to address the issue for Microsoft Installer-based Office 2016, but the fix does not apply to Office 2016 Click-to-Run editions.
  • 03The reported issue also affects Excel Online and Excel 2024, 2021, 2019, and 2016, while Microsoft advised affected users to use Paste Special until a permanent solution is available.
  • 04Users can uninstall KB5002914 to restore copy-and-paste functionality, but doing so removes patches for remote code execution and information disclosure vulnerabilities.

Microsoft said its September 2026 KB5002914 security update introduced a code regression that can cause Excel copy-and-paste operations, autofill, and formula dragging to fail silently. When the problem occurs, the source content remains selected while the destination is unchanged, with no error message or beep. The issue was reported by customers on Microsoft Q&A and Reddit and affects Excel Online as well as Excel 2024, 2021, 2019, and 2016.

Microsoft released KB5002665 to mitigate the problem, but the update only fixes MSI-based Office 2016 installations and does not apply to Office 2016 Click-to-Run editions such as Microsoft Office 365 Home. Until broader fixes are available, Microsoft recommends using Paste Special and selecting the desired paste type with Ctrl+Alt+V. Uninstalling KB5002914 has also restored functionality for some users, but Microsoft warns that doing so removes patches for remote code execution and information disclosure vulnerabilities.

  • The failure can be difficult to detect because Excel leaves the source selected and provides no beep or error message while the destination remains unchanged.
  • KB5002665 is limited to MSI-based Office 2016, so users of Office 2016 Click-to-Run editions, including Microsoft Office 365 Home, are not covered by that fix.
  • Microsoft's interim workaround is Paste Special, which lets users choose specific content types such as formulas, values, number formats, or links rather than using standard paste.
  • Rolling back KB5002914 may restore normal Excel behavior, but it also removes fixes for remote code execution and information disclosure issues.

A September Microsoft update caused some Excel users to find that copying, pasting, filling cells, or dragging formulas appeared to work but changed nothing. Microsoft has issued a fix for the installer-based version of Office 2016, but people using Excel online and several newer Excel versions may need to use a different paste option until a broader fix arrives. Removing the problematic update can restore copying and pasting, but it also removes fixes for security flaws that could let others run harmful code or view protected information.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a specific Microsoft Office update regression with a limited fix and a potentially consequential rollback tradeoff, since uninstalling KB5002914 removes security patches. It is most relevant to professionals supporting affected Office deployments, but it does not report active exploitation or a newly disclosed security vulnerability.

Varonis describes building its Triage Agent, an AI system intended to investigate security alerts before a human analyst reviews them. The agent draws on the company’s Data Security Platform for context about identities, permissions, sensitive data, behavioral patterns, and related events. Air Security reported a flaw called Plugin4Shell in Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Google Gemini CLI. The flaw can let someone who controls a plugin repository replace a plugin’s code even when the agent says it is installing a specific reviewed version. The replacement can run with the user’s access, including access to files, saved credentials, and systems the user can log in to.

The issue arises because the agents retrieve a commit identified by a fixed code string but do not verify that the resulting code actually matches that identifier. On Git hosts that allow a branch to be named like a commit identifier, a repository owner can redirect that branch to different code while the agent continues reporting the pinned version.   • Background plugin updates could allow a previously trusted plugin to be replaced without a new prompt, but the article says default auto-updating marketplaces for Claude Code and Codex are GitHub-hosted and therefore not exposed to the hash-like branch method.
  • Gemini CLI can reportedly be targeted through a differently named main branch, FETCH_HEAD, so GitHub’s restriction on hash-like branch names does not clearly rule out exposure for Gemini CLI plugins.
  • Because verification occurs on the user’s machine, the article says marketplaces cannot correct the issue for existing users; a fix must be delivered in the coding agent itself.

A flaw in four AI tools used for writing code can let the owner of a plugin’s online code repository quietly replace a reviewed plugin with harmful code. This can affect people who install plugins from services that allow specially named code branches, while the default plugin catalogs for Claude Code and GitHub Copilot use GitHub and are not exposed to this version of the problem. A malicious replacement could access a user’s files, saved passwords, and systems they can reach, making it important to update Claude Code or Codex; GitHub Copilot has no fix, and Google reportedly will not fix Gemini CLI.

Researchers at Zimperium have identified RatHat, an Android malware assessed to be operated by China-based threat actors. It is distributed through targeted text-message phishing, malicious advertisements, deceptive download portals, and third-party forums that prompt users to install malicious APK files. The initial app acts as a dropper and includes several anti-analysis measures intended to hinder automated inspection.

RatHat abuses Android Accessibility permissions to unlock Developer Options, enable Wireless Debugging, and obtain an Android Debug Bridge pairing code. It then uses local Android Debug Bridge access to run a Go-based agent with shell-level privileges and an FRP reverse tunnel that gives operators continuing access to the device. This access can remain after the malicious app is uninstalled, and the separate component can check whether the app is present and reinstall it.

Zimperium said the combination of independently running components, persistent device access, and real-time AI decision loops makes signature-based mobile security controls insufficient.

Researchers found a new Android threat called RatHat that is spread through fake download sites, deceptive ads, and text-message scams that trick people into installing harmful apps. Attackers turned a genuine Dell order acknowledgement into a callback-phishing lure by placing a fraudulent order, then relaying the vendor-signed email through Microsoft 365 tenants to unrelated targets. DKIM and DMARC passed because the message was authentic, but its signed recipient field showed it was originally addressed to an attacker-controlled mailbox—not the final recipient.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Attackers submitted a Dell order using an attacker-controlled Microsoft 365 mailbox, causing Dell to generate and sign a genuine order acknowledgement and PDF.
  • 02The same signed message was relayed through different second-hop Microsoft 365 tenants to two unrelated organizations about two minutes apart, while its signature, message identifier, attachment hash, and purchase identifier remained identical.
  • 03The final messages passed sender-policy, DKIM, DMARC, and composite authentication checks because relaying changed the delivery envelope without altering the signed message content.
  • 04The signed recipient field still named the attacker-controlled tenant rather than the final recipient, providing evidence that the message was not originally generated for the receiving mailbox.
  • 05The order’s shipping and billing address fields contained a helpline phone number and sales-language text, making the phone number the only actionable content in an otherwise genuine Dell receipt.

Attackers submitted a Dell order using the attacker-controlled mailbox no-reply@Dynamic535[.]onmicrosoft[.]com, causing Dell to generate a genuine signed order acknowledgement and PDF. The same signed email was then relayed through different Microsoft 365 tenants to a commercial cleaning and property restoration franchise organization and an unrelated professional-services firm about two minutes apart. The delivered copies shared the same signature value, message identifier, attachment hash, purchase identifier, and outbound gateway tracking identifier. Neither recipient organization had placed the order.

The messages passed sender-policy, DKIM, DMARC, and composite authentication checks because relaying changed only the SMTP delivery envelope rather than the signed headers or body. However, the signed recipient field still named the attacker-controlled tenant mailbox, not the final recipient, and the article notes that DMARC does not evaluate this mismatch. The only actionable lure was a phone number inserted into the order’s shipping and billing address fields alongside text such as “Helpline” and “Call Our Sales Team”; all links and the attached Dell PDF were clean. The article reports that two human reviewers marked the messages malicious after an automated analyst initially considered clean authentication and artifact scans more important than the recipient’s report that no order had been made.

  • A valid signature can prove that Dell generated the message while still failing to prove that Dell intended it for the person who ultimately received it, because the signed recipient field named a different mailbox and DMARC does not assess that mismatch.
  • The campaign needed no malicious website, attachment, or altered email content: the actionable callback lure was placed in structured shipping and billing address fields that Dell’s own order system rendered.
  • Using separate relay tenants for different targets allowed the same vendor-signed message to be distributed to unrelated organizations while preserving the original signed content.
  • Dell’s normal order, shipping, and delivery automation supplied follow-up messages across multiple lifecycle stages, giving the operation an authentic-looking cadence without attackers composing new brand-themed emails.
  • The article shows that an employee reporting an order they did not make and a first-time transactional message can be stronger practical warning signs than clean authentication and artifact scans.

Scammers placed a fake Dell order and used Dell’s real order-confirmation email, including its genuine invoice, to tell people at two unrelated companies to call a phone number hidden in the shipping address. The email looked trustworthy because Dell really sent it and it passed normal checks meant to confirm who sent it, even though neither company had made the purchase. This matters because criminals can use legitimate companies’ automated emails to bypass common filters and persuade employees to call scammers, without needing a malicious link or file.

Trail of Bits used AI agents to build MASM developer tooling, static analyses, and Lean formal models before auditing the Miden zkVM, enabling deeper review of an unfamiliar assembly ecosystem. KEY POINTS
  • 01Trail of Bits spent six months preparing to audit the Miden VM by using AI agents to build MASM tooling, including an LSP server, decompiler, static-analysis engine, and Lean model of the VM executor.
  • 02The static analyses identified more than 400 reachable locations in the Miden core library where type validation could be improved.

Trail of Bits prepared for an audit of the Miden VM by using AI agents over six months to build developer and review tooling for Miden assembly, a custom stack-based language with little existing tooling. The resulting projects included an LSP server, a decompiler, a static-analysis engine, and a Lean model of the VM executor. The team used Claude for planning and development and Codex for review, with generated results tested against MASM procedures and regressions added as tests.

The static analyses found more than 400 reachable locations where type validation could be improved, along with a high-severity issue in the mod_12289 procedure. A prover-controlled remainder was not validated before use, enabling carefully chosen inputs to produce an incorrect modular result and potentially let a malicious prover forge Falcon signatures and drain Miden accounts controlled by Falcon keys. The formal-modeling work produced 95 machine-checked correctness proofs for the library’s binary arithmetic components and identified two further bugs in rotr and wrapping_mul that the unit tests had missed.

  • The decompiler’s most valuable outcome was not necessarily readable decompiled code, but the internal representation and analysis framework that could be reused to build static security checks.
  • Because MASM procedures often lack declared inputs, consistent calling conventions, and stack-neutral control flow, the team deliberately targeted a well-defined subset for correct decompilation rather than attempting incomplete coverage of all procedures.
  • Machine-checked Lean proofs reduced the manual review burden to checking whether each theorem described the intended behavior, because the Lean kernel verified that the proofs themselves were valid.
  • Most of the more than 400 type-validation findings were reachable because nearly all core-library procedures were public, allowing third-party developers to invoke them without proper validation.
  • The article argues that AI agents changed the economics of exploratory audit preparation: projects that previously could not be justified in advance can now be pursued with light supervision, with failed side projects primarily costing tokens.

Trail of Bits used AI helpers to build tools for checking Miden, a new system designed to run programs with strong privacy protections, before its launch. The tools found a serious flaw that could have let a dishonest user forge Falcon digital signatures and steal money from Miden accounts using those keys. They also found two smaller programming mistakes and created 95 computer-checked proofs that parts of the system worked as intended. This matters because AI-assisted preparation can help security reviewers find costly flaws in new, complex software that otherwise has little existing support for testing and inspection.

Unit 42 found that AWS AgentCore Harness’s default shell tool can be steered via prompt injection to run code as root, read the harness process memory, and extract plaintext credentials resolved from AgentCore Identity. KEY POINTS
  • 01Unit 42 reported that AWS AgentCore Harness provides built-in shell and file-operation tools by default unless operators restrict them with the allowedTools parameter at invocation time.
  • 02In the researchers’ test environment, an indirect prompt injection embedded in a support ticket caused the harness to download and execute a script through its shell tool.
  • 03The researchers found that the shell tool ran as root and could read the memory of the harness runtime process, where AgentCore Identity credentials had been resolved into plaintext.
  • 04The test script extracted an Amazon Cognito bearer token and the connected MCP server URL from process memory, then sent them to a simulated attacker-controlled endpoint.
  • 05AWS closed the report as informative under its AgentCore shared-responsibility model and identified tool scoping and outbound-network filtering as customer-side controls.

Unit 42 researchers found that default AWS AgentCore Harness configurations can let an attacker use prompt injection to steer an AI agent into exposing plaintext credentials managed by AgentCore Identity. The issue centers on the harness’s built-in shell and file-operation tools, which are available in each session unless restricted with allowedTools. AWS reviewed the report and closed it as informative under its AgentCore shared-responsibility model, identifying tool scoping and outbound-network filtering as customer-managed controls.

In the researchers’ test, a hidden instruction in a simulated support ticket persuaded the agent to download and run a script through the shell tool. The shell ran as root and could read the memory of the harness runtime process, where an AgentCore Identity reference had been turned into a usable Amazon Cognito bearer token. The script extracted both that token and the connected MCP server address, then sent them to a simulated attacker endpoint.

The researchers replayed the extracted credential from a laptop without AWS credentials and used the test MCP server to retrieve customer information and create a ticket. They emphasized that the stolen token belonged to the operator’s reusable downstream service account, rather than the user who invoked the harness. Unit 42 recommends restricting tools at invocation time, limiting service-account permissions, and monitoring outbound traffic from harness containers.

  • The credential exposed in the demonstration was not the person invoking the agent’s short-lived login token, but the operator’s reusable downstream-service account token, which could carry access the caller was never meant to have.
  • Encrypting credentials in storage and while they travel does not protect them once the runtime must turn them into usable plaintext; the article demonstrated that a same-privilege shell could retrieve that plaintext from memory.
  • The article notes that allowedTools is applied when invoking a harness rather than when creating it, making per-session tool restriction important because the default shell and file tools otherwise remain available.
  • The extracted token was replayable from the researchers’ laptop without AWS credentials, allowing access to the test MCP server’s customer lookup and ticket-creation capabilities.
  • The article frames unrestricted outbound network access as a practical exfiltration path: a harness contacting a destination outside its approved downstream integrations can indicate an active prompt-injection attempt.

Researchers found that an AI customer-support system built with AWS AgentCore can be tricked by hidden instructions in a support ticket into running unwanted commands. Those commands could pull a login token from the system’s working memory and let an attacker use it to access connected services and customer information. This matters to organizations using this setup because a single malicious message could give someone the same access as the organization’s own automated service account.

Elastic describes using Cross-Project Search (CPS) in Elastic Cloud Serverless to centralize security monitoring across separate projects while leaving data in each project. One Elastic Security origin project can run detection rules against data in linked projects, placing resulting alerts, cases, and investigations in a single origin-based queue. The company tested this model with one origin linked to 100 projects and roughly 2,100 prebuilt detection rules.

The test found that analyst query patterns remained interactive, with query cost driven more by per-project data volume and query design than by the number of linked projects. Elastic recommends selecting only necessary fields in ES|QL queries, enabling rules that analysts will actually review, and using alert suppression for noisy rules. CPS is read-only across project boundaries, so analysts can investigate centrally but must perform actions such as closing alerts, isolating hosts, and running osquery in the project that owns the data.

  • At 100 linked projects, query cost was driven more by the amount of data in each project and the query shape than by the number of linked projects, making quiet projects comparatively inexpensive to include.
  • Retrieving complete documents at scale was much slower than selecting only needed fields, so the article recommends limiting returned fields for interactive investigations and reserving full-document retrieval for exports.
  • Rules automatically cover all linked projects, but a rule can search only projects its most recent editor is allowed to access, so rule creation and updates require an identity with access across the intended projects.
  • The maximum number of alerts allowed per rule run applies to the rule's entire cross-project scope, meaning noisy rules can reach that limit more easily as the number of linked projects grows; suppression and per-rule tuning are therefore important.

Elastic describes testing a setup where one central security team monitored alerts from 100 separate projects while each project kept control of its own data. This can help organizations managing different teams, regions, or customers avoid copying the same monitoring rules and forcing analysts to switch between many separate systems. The central team can review and investigate possible threats in one place, but actions such as isolating a computer must still be carried out within the project that owns it, helping preserve separation between customers or teams.

SHOULD · 85 news 18 Sep 2026 18:46 UTC · gpt-5.6-terra

Happy Birthday, Shai-Hulud

One year after the first npm Shai-Hulud compromise, its credential-stealing, self-propagating supply-chain technique has evolved into repeated waves run by multiple actors, aided by publicly released code and CI token hijacking. Although two alleged TeamPCP members were arrested, the original worm’s authors remain unidentified and the threat persists across the npm ecosystem.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A malicious version of @ctrl/tinycolor published to npm in September 2025 initiated the first known self-propagating worm in the npm ecosystem, which spread into dozens of packages and CrowdStrike’s npm namespace.
  • 02The Shai-Hulud payload used TruffleHog to find npm tokens, GitHub credentials, and cloud keys, sent discovered secrets to attacker-controlled locations, added a GitHub Actions workflow for persistence, and republished itself using stolen npm tokens.
  • 03A November 2025 wave moved execution to the pre-install step, introduced setup_bun.js and bun_environment.js, and included a fallback that could attempt to wipe a user’s home directory.
  • 04Later 2026 campaigns used publicly released Shai-Hulud source code, including a May burst that pushed more than 400 malicious versions across 172 packages by hijacking short-lived OIDC tokens from CI.
  • 05Australian Federal Police arrested two men in Western Australia on August 26, 2026 over alleged TeamPCP involvement, but the original authors of the September and November 2025 Shai-Hulud attacks remain unidentified.

A malicious version of @ctrl/tinycolor published to npm in September 2025 launched the first known self-propagating worm in the npm ecosystem. The Shai-Hulud payload used TruffleHog to search for npm tokens, GitHub credentials, and cloud keys, sent stolen secrets to attacker-controlled locations, and used stolen npm tokens to infect and republish other packages. It also created a GitHub Actions workflow for persistence, and researchers ultimately counted compromised packages in the hundreds.

Later waves expanded the threat through pre-install execution, new payloads, and a destructive fallback that could attempt to wipe a user’s home directory. In 2026, TeamPCP released source code for a Shai-Hulud worm framework, while multiple operators began running similar campaigns; one May burst pushed more than 400 malicious versions across 172 packages by hijacking short-lived OIDC tokens from CI. Australian police arrested two alleged TeamPCP members in August 2026, but the original authors of the September and November 2025 attacks remain unidentified, and the publicly copied code continues to enable new campaigns.

  • The threat evolved beyond stolen long-lived credentials: one May 2026 wave spread through hijacked short-lived OIDC tokens from CI systems, showing that short-lived access tokens did not prevent that campaign.
  • Moving malicious code to the pre-install step in November 2025 expanded exposure from package users to developer machines and automated build pipelines before installation completed.
  • TeamPCP’s release of the worm’s source code in May 2026 lowered the barrier for other operators, and the article reports that multiple actors were running Shai-Hulud-style campaigns by mid-2026.
  • Arrests of alleged TeamPCP operators do not resolve attribution for the original Shai-Hulud incidents, because the September and November 2025 attacks were never definitively linked to TeamPCP.

The article looks back at Shai-Hulud, a malicious program that spread through npm, a widely used source of software building blocks, after criminals took over trusted packages such as tinycolor. It searched developers’ computers and automated build systems for passwords and access keys, then used those keys to infect more packages and potentially steal data or damage files. Hundreds of packages and more than a thousand organizations were affected over repeated waves, while many developers had to repeatedly replace access keys and check their software. Although police arrested two people allegedly tied to later attacks, the original creators are unknown and the code has been widely copied, making future incidents easier for others to carry out.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This retrospective documents a high-impact, ongoing npm supply-chain threat that repeatedly compromised hundreds of packages through credential theft and CI token hijacking. It also covers the arrest of alleged TeamPCP operators while emphasizing that the original authors remain unidentified and the publicly released worm code continues to enable new campaigns.

Optional · 48 opinion 18 Sep 2026 04:05 UTC · gpt-5.6-terra

Notes from a CISO: Rethinking Risk Acceptance in the AI Era

AI is making existing security weaknesses faster and cheaper to discover, chain, and exploit, so organizations must reassess previously accepted risks. Strong least-privilege access, segmentation, bounded AI-agent permissions, continuous validation, and faster monitored response are increasingly essential.
KEY POINTS
  • 01AI can make existing weaknesses, such as excessive permissions, exposed identities, misconfigurations, known vulnerabilities, and weak segmentation, faster and cheaper to discover and exploit at scale.
  • 02Organizations should reassess risks that were accepted because they were considered difficult to discover, chain, or exploit, since AI is weakening those assumptions.
  • 03AI agents should have distinct, limited identities, explicit tools, restricted data access, clear action permissions, and reliable ways to revoke their access.
  • 04AI-assisted security workflows can help identify requirements, sensitive data flows, abuse cases, trust assumptions, and implementation issues earlier in the engineering lifecycle.
  • 05Monitoring and incident response need sufficient identity, cloud, endpoint, application, and data context to distinguish expected automation from unauthorized or unsafe activity.

AI is changing the assumptions behind many accepted security risks by making existing weaknesses faster and cheaper to find, connect, and exploit. The article argues that attackers often do not need novel techniques when excessive permissions, exposed identities, misconfigurations, known vulnerabilities, or weak network separation provide an easier path. A compromised identity with broad file access, for example, can be used with AI-assisted analysis to quickly identify sensitive and relevant information. Organizations should reassess risks that were accepted because they were considered difficult to discover, chain, or exploit at scale.

The article emphasizes foundational controls such as least-privilege access, network separation, managed devices, controlled connectivity, privileged access management, and time-limited elevated access. AI agents should have bounded identities, explicit tools, restricted data and action permissions, and a reliable way to remove their access rather than inheriting broad authority. AI can also help extend security work across planning, architecture, implementation, testing, monitoring, and incident response, but human review, accountability, audit trails, and controlled approval for high-impact actions remain necessary. Continuous validation should focus on controls likely to change as infrastructure, permissions, integrations, agent capabilities, and threat information evolve.

  • The article argues that AI’s most immediate effect may be reducing the effort needed to exploit familiar weaknesses rather than requiring attackers to find novel vulnerabilities.
  • A compromised account with broad access can become far more dangerous when AI can rapidly sort, classify, and connect accessible information to identify valuable targets.
  • Security reviews should be triggered by meaningful changes—such as permission drift, new integrations, expanded agent capabilities, or new threat information—rather than treated as one-time approval exercises.
  • Giving an AI agent the same broad authority as the person or service that launched it is presented as a preventable source of excessive risk; its access should instead match a specific task and expire where possible.
  • Adding AI to an existing alert queue is not enough to improve response speed; it must help connect evidence, reconstruct events, identify affected assets, and support controlled containment actions.

The article argues that AI makes it faster and cheaper for criminals to find and combine security gaps that companies may have previously considered low risk. Businesses using AI tools, especially ones that can access company files, code, or internal systems, could face greater harm if an account or device is compromised. Organizations need to limit what each person and AI tool can access, regularly check that protections still work, and respond quickly when suspicious activity appears. The broader risk is that one weak account, setting, or poorly controlled AI tool could turn into a much larger company-wide incident.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a broad best-practice perspective on reassessing accepted security risks as AI reduces the cost of discovery, chaining, and exploitation. It provides useful strategic guidance but does not report a specific incident, active threat, vulnerability, or urgent remediation.

Optional · 30 announcement 18 Sep 2026 15:54 UTC · gpt-5.6-terra

What scales when headcount doubles

As IT teams grow from supporting dozens to hundreds of employees, informal processes held together by individual knowledge fail first. The presentation discusses how to decide which workflows to automate, outsource, or retain manually across device operations, identity, support, security, and compliance.
KEY POINTS
  • 01As companies grow from roughly 80 to 400 employees, IT must shift from relying on one person to operating as a repeatable system.
  • 02Scaling IT increases ticket volume and makes identity management, compliance, documentation, and device operations more complex.
  • 03Processes that depend on one person’s judgment or memory are likely failure points as an organization grows.
  • 04Device-management tools can automate enrollment and configuration, but forecasting, sourcing, storing, shipping, retrieving, and retiring devices still require separate processes.
  • 05The presentation features Teamworks security and IT leader Joe Hurshman discussing which IT operations to systematize, hand off, or leave manual.

The article previews a presentation about how IT operations must change as an organization grows from about 80 employees to 400. It describes routine problems that expose weak processes, such as unclear account-provisioning ownership, unavailable evidence for security questionnaires, and difficulty supplying a laptop to an employee in another region. The presentation argues that IT must become a system rather than rely on a single person’s knowledge and judgment.

As growth increases ticket volume, identity and access work, compliance demands, documentation gaps, and device logistics, teams must decide what to formalize, hand to a partner, or leave manual. The article notes that tools can automate well-defined parts of a process, such as device enrollment and configuration, while tasks including forecasting, sourcing, shipping, retrieval, and retirement remain outside device management. Joe Hurshman, who runs security and IT at Teamworks, will discuss what he systematized, delegated, or left alone across different stages of company growth. The presentation also includes an attendee question session focused on specific real-world operational problems.

  • A practical way to find scaling risks is to identify every workflow where the answer to "how does this happen?" is a particular person rather than a defined process.
  • IT tools tend to automate the clearly defined middle of a workflow while leaving operational edge tasks, such as device shipping and retirement, unresolved.
  • The core prioritization decision during growth is not to automate everything, but to determine which work should receive a system, be handled by a partner, or remain manual.
  • Organizational transitions often occur without planning while IT is occupied with daily work, making operational weaknesses easy to miss until a routine request exposes them.

This article previews a presentation about how IT work changes when a company grows from a small team to hundreds of employees, featuring Teamworks security and IT leader Joe Hurshman. Growing companies can struggle with setting up accounts, supplying laptops in different regions, answering security questions, and keeping records current when tasks depend on one person’s memory. It matters because inconsistent or unclear processes can delay new employees, create operational problems, and make it harder for a business to meet security and compliance expectations.

This is an event preview and evergreen discussion of IT scaling practices rather than reporting a specific security incident, vulnerability, or urgent finding. It may be useful for operational planning, but it is low priority for immediate security awareness.

Chat is real-time text communication between people or between a person and a software system.
also: chats
Check Point organization
Check Point is a cybersecurity company known for firewall, network security, cloud security, and threat prevention products.
Check Point Security Management Server product
Check Point Security Management Server is the central server used to manage Check Point security gateways and policies.
Check Point Software organization
Check Point Software is a cybersecurity company known for firewalls, threat prevention, and security research.
china
China is a country often referenced in cybersecurity reporting involving technology, espionage, regulation, and threat activity.
also: China-based
Chrome product
A popular web browser developed by Google, frequently targeted by exploit kits and phishing campaigns.
Chrome browser product
Chrome browser is Google's widely used web browser.
Chrome extension product
A Chrome extension is a small add-on that changes or adds features to the Google Chrome browser.
Chrome Extension Storage concept
Chrome extension storage is data saved by browser extensions, such as settings, tokens, or other extension information.
CI concept
A software development practice where code changes are regularly merged and tested automatically.
CI pipelines concept
CI pipelines are automated steps that build and test code whenever developers make changes.
CI/CD concept
CI/CD is a software delivery approach that automatically builds, tests, and deploys code changes.
CI/CD Secrets concept
Sensitive passwords, keys, or tokens used by automated software building and deployment systems.
CircleCI product
CircleCI is a cloud service that automatically builds, tests, and deploys software projects.
cisa organization
CISA is the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which helps protect critical infrastructure and shares security guidance.
also: CISA guidance
claude
Claude is Anthropic’s family of AI assistants and language models.
claude-code
Claude Code is Anthropic’s AI coding assistant for helping developers write and manage software projects.

Click2Shell is the name given to a WordPress vulnerability that can trick an administrator's browser into installing a theme.
clickfix

Client platforms product
Client platforms are user-facing devices or operating systems, such as laptops, desktops, or phones, that connect to services.
Clipboard Contents concept
Clipboard contents are the text, files, or other data a person has copied and may later paste.
clipboard data concept
Clipboard data is the text, images, or other content temporarily stored when a user copies or cuts something on a computer or phone.
clipboard-logging technique
Clipboard logging is the collection of data that users copy to their computer clipboard.
cloud concept
The cloud is internet-based computing where data and applications run on remote servers instead of only on your own device.
cloud environments concept
Cloud environments are computing systems and services run in cloud platforms rather than on local machines.
cloud keys concept
Digital credentials used to access cloud accounts, services, or resources.
CloudTrail product
CloudTrail is an AWS service that records management API activity.
also: CloudTrail events
code execution technique
Code execution means an attacker can make a computer or server run commands or software of their choosing.
Code Regression concept
A new software bug caused when a change makes a feature that previously worked stop working correctly.
Code repositories concept
Code repositories are storage locations where software source code and its change history are kept.
code repository tool
A code repository is an online or local storage place where software source code and its change history are kept.
codex
Codex is an OpenAI AI coding model or coding assistant technology for helping write and understand code.
coding concept
Coding is writing instructions in a programming language so a computer can perform tasks.
coding agent tool
A coding agent is an AI-powered tool that can help write, edit, or run software code on a user's behalf.
Collaboration concept
Collaboration means people or organizations working together, often by sharing information, systems, or responsibilities.
Collaboration platforms product
Collaboration platforms are apps such as chat, document, and meeting tools that help people work together online.
command injection technique
Command injection is an attack where someone tricks an application into running system commands chosen by the attacker.

A command server is an attacker-controlled system that sends instructions to malware or compromised devices.

Command-and-control is the way attackers remotely send instructions to malware and receive data back from infected machines.
command-and-control infrastructure concept
Command-and-control infrastructure is the servers and systems attackers use to send instructions to malware and receive stolen data.
Commit Hash concept
A commit hash is a unique code that identifies one exact saved version of source code.
Compensating controls concept
Alternative security measures used to reduce risk when a preferred control cannot be put in place.
Complete control concept
Complete control means an attacker can fully manage a system, account, or application as if they owned it.

Composite authentication is using several identity or message-checking signals together to decide whether something is trustworthy.
also: composite authentication pass, maximum reason code
compromise concept
A compromise is a situation where a system, account, or data has been breached or taken over by an attacker.
compromised concept
Compromised means a system, account, or device has been accessed or controlled by someone who should not have access.
compromised account concept
An account whose credentials have been stolen or guessed, allowing an attacker to impersonate the legitimate user.
compromised identity concept
A compromised identity is an account or digital identity that an attacker has taken control of or can use without permission.
Conditional Redirects technique
Conditional redirects send visitors to different web pages depending on conditions such as their device, location, or browser.
confidential information concept
Confidential information is private or sensitive data that should only be shared with authorized people.
configuration information concept
Settings and parameters that determine how software or a device behaves.
Connected Applications concept
Applications that have been linked to an account or service so they can access data or perform actions.
Contagious Interview technique
Contagious Interview is a North Korea-linked campaign that tricks job seekers or developers into running malicious software during fake interviews.
container concept
A container is a lightweight package that runs an application with its needed files in an isolated environment.
container escape technique
A container escape is when an attacker breaks out of an isolated software container to access the underlying host system.
Container Tampering technique
A technique that alters the contents or metadata of a software package so different tools interpret it differently.
containers concept
Containers are lightweight packages that run applications with their needed files in isolated environments.
containment technique
Containment is the process of limiting a cyber incident so attackers or malware cannot spread further.
Content Delivery Network concept
A Content Delivery Network is a group of servers that deliver websites and files faster by serving them from locations near users.
Content Security Policy protocol
Content Security Policy is a browser security feature that helps websites limit what scripts, images, forms, and other content are allowed to load or run.
Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only protocol
Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only is a browser security-header mode that reports policy violations without blocking anything.
continuous assurance concept
Continuous assurance is the ongoing checking of security controls and evidence instead of relying only on occasional audits.
Continuous Validation concept
Continuous validation means repeatedly checking that security controls, identities, or systems still work as expected instead of testing them only once.
control flow concept
Control flow is the order in which a program’s instructions run, including branches, loops, and function calls.
controlled connectivity concept
Controlled connectivity is a security approach that limits which systems, services, or agents are allowed to connect to one another.
Controlled endpoint concept
A controlled endpoint is a server, device, or URL that a tester or attacker controls and can monitor or change.
cookies concept
Cookies are small pieces of data websites store in a browser to remember logins, settings, or tracking information.
Copilot product
Copilot is Microsoft's AI assistant built into various Microsoft products to help with tasks like writing, searching, and coding.
copy and paste concept
A common computer action that duplicates selected content and places it somewhere else.
Copy-paste technique
Copy-paste is the everyday action of copying text or data from one place and inserting it somewhere else.
Corelight organization
Corelight is a cybersecurity company that provides network detection and response products.
corporate networks concept
Corporate networks are the connected computers, servers, and systems used by a company.
Correctness Proofs technique
Correctness proofs are mathematical demonstrations that software or an algorithm behaves as intended under defined assumptions.
Correlations tool
A security feature that links related alerts, events, or findings to help analysts investigate them together.
Cosense product
Cosense is an online service operated by Helpfeel.
Counter Adversary Operations organization
CrowdStrike's team that investigates and tracks cyber threat actors and their attacks.
Crafted link technique
A specially constructed web link intended to cause a program or person to perform an attacker-chosen action.
CreateAccessKey technique
An AWS API action that creates a new access key for an IAM user.
credential concept
A credential is proof of identity for logging in, such as a password, security token, API key, or certificate.
credential theft technique
Credential theft is the stealing of usernames, passwords, tokens, or other login information.
credential-exfiltration technique
Credential-exfiltration is the theft and removal of usernames, passwords, tokens, or keys from a system.
credential-stealing technique
Credential-stealing is the act of stealing login details such as passwords, session cookies, or access tokens.
credentials concept
Credentials are login details or access tokens that prove a user or system is allowed to access something.
Credentials and Secrets concept
Sensitive values, such as passwords, API keys, and tokens, that prove identity or grant access to systems.

A search capability that lets one system query data stored in multiple separate clusters.
also: CCS

A search capability that lets a central project query data held by other connected projects without copying it first.
also: CPS, cross-project scope
crowdstrike organization
CrowdStrike is a cybersecurity company known for endpoint protection, threat intelligence, and incident response.
also: CrowdStrike's npm namespace
cryptocurrency concept
Cryptocurrency is digital money, such as Bitcoin, that uses cryptography and usually runs on a blockchain.
cryptocurrency wallet product
A cryptocurrency wallet is software or hardware used to store and use the keys that control digital coins.
Cryptocurrency wallet credentials concept
Secret login information or recovery data that can give someone access to a cryptocurrency wallet.
cryptocurrency wallet data concept
Information about cryptocurrency wallets, including keys, balances, and transaction history, often targeted by thieves.
cryptocurrency wallet extensions product
Cryptocurrency wallet extensions are browser add-ons that help users store, send, or manage digital currency keys and transactions.
cryptocurrency wallets product
Cryptocurrency wallets are tools used to store and manage access to digital currency funds.

CSPM, or Cloud Security Posture Management, is software that checks cloud environments for risky settings and compliance problems.
Ctrl+Alt+V concept
A keyboard shortcut commonly used in Microsoft Office to open Paste Special options.
customer information concept
Customer information is data a business keeps about its customers, such as names, contact details, purchases, or account records.

The WordPress Customizer is a feature for previewing and changing a website theme's appearance.

A CVSS score is a standard number used to show how severe a software vulnerability is.
cyber actors concept

cyberespionage technique
The use of computer networks to conduct espionage, usually by state-sponsored groups to steal secrets from governments or corporations.
Dangerous, high-risk file attachments concept
Files sent with a message that may contain malware or otherwise harm a device or account.
also: file attachments
data exfiltration technique
Data exfiltration is the unauthorized removal or copying of data from a system.
data flow concept
A data flow is the path information takes as it moves between people, applications, devices, and storage systems.
also: data flows

also: DSP
data theft concept
Data theft is the stealing of information from a system or service.

Data transfers are movements of information from one person, system, company, or country to another.

A security research group referenced in reporting on malicious software packages.
debugging technique
Debugging is the process of finding and fixing problems in software code.

decompiled technique

defaced technique

Defender usually refers to Microsoft Defender, Microsoft’s built-in security and antimalware product line.

The Defender portal is Microsoft’s web console for viewing and managing Microsoft Defender security alerts and settings.

The Defense Department is the U.S. government department responsible for the military and national defense.
delegate concept

deleted concept
Deleted means removed from normal access, though copies may sometimes still exist in backups, logs, or recovery areas.
Dell organization
A major technology company known for personal computers, servers, and IT equipment.
also: vendor, brand
Delphos Labs organization
Delphos Labs is a cybersecurity research organization.
dependencies concept
Dependencies are outside software components that a project relies on to work.

Detect means to identify suspicious or malicious activity in systems, networks, or data.
detection concept
Detection is the process of finding signs of suspicious or malicious activity.
detection engineers concept

A detection rule is a set of instructions a security tool uses to spot suspicious activity or known threats.

Detection rules are instructions security tools use to flag suspicious behavior or known attack patterns.

The tools, settings, accounts, and files a software developer uses to create and test programs.

Device operations are the day-to-day tasks of obtaining, preparing, shipping, supporting, and replacing employee devices.

An Elastic interface for searching and exploring collected data and events.

Discovery is the attacker activity of learning about a victim’s systems, accounts, and network before taking further action.
disruption concept
Disruption is an interruption that prevents systems, services, or operations from working normally.
disruptive concept
Disruptive describes activity that interrupts normal use of a system, service, or business process.

The Netherlands government organization that provides cybersecurity advice, warnings, and incident-response support.

Earth Karkaddan threat-actor
A threat-actor group referenced in security reporting.
egress concept

Elastic Cloud Hosted product
Elastic's cloud-hosted service for running its search, analytics, and security products.
Elastic Cloud Serverless product
A cloud service from Elastic that runs search, observability, and security workloads without the user managing the underlying servers.

also: Security

element_width concept
A code-field setting that specifies the width of data elements in certain Android DEX instructions.

To gain higher-level permissions on a system than a user or attacker originally had.
elevated access concept
Elevated access means a user or program has higher-than-normal permissions, such as administrator rights.
elevated privileges concept
Higher access rights than a standard user, allowing actions like installing software or modifying system files.
email addresses concept
Email addresses are the unique names people use to send and receive email, such as user@example.com.

Email security protects inboxes and users from threats such as phishing, malware, and scam messages.
email systems concept
Email systems are the services and software that send, receive, store, and manage email messages.
employers organization
Employers are people or organizations that hire workers and may hold sensitive employee information.
encrypted concept
Encrypted data has been scrambled so that only someone with the right key can read it.
encrypted communications concept
Encrypted communications are messages protected so outsiders cannot easily read them.
encryption concept
Encryption is a way of scrambling information so only someone with the right key can read it.

Encryption keys are secret values used to lock and unlock protected data.

End to end means something is handled across the whole process from start to finish, often without gaps between steps.

End-users are the people who actually use a system, app, or service.
endpoint concept
An endpoint is a user device such as a laptop, phone, or server that connects to a network.

Entry points are the places where attackers can first get into a system or network.

environment variables concept
Environment variables are named settings stored by an operating system or runtime that programs can read while they run.

To escalate privileges means to gain higher-level access on a system than you were originally allowed to have.
espionage concept
Espionage is spying to gather information without permission.

Excel is Microsoft’s spreadsheet application for organizing and analyzing data.
Excel 2024 product
A desktop version of Microsoft's Excel spreadsheet program released in 2024.
Excel Online product
The web-browser version of Microsoft Excel.

A file extension on Windows that runs an executable program, commonly used to install software but also to deliver malware.
executable concept
An executable is a file that can run as a program on a computer.

Execute code means to make a computer run instructions, which is dangerous if an attacker can run their own code.

Execution is the stage where an attacker runs code or commands on a target system.
exfiltration technique

exploit technique

exploit kit tool
An exploit kit is a package of tools criminals use to automatically find and exploit vulnerable browsers, plugins, or systems.
exploitation technique
Exploitation is taking advantage of a weakness in software or people to gain unauthorized access or control.
exploitation attempts technique
Exploitation attempts are tries to take advantage of a software weakness to gain access, run code, or cause harm.
Exploitation in the wild concept
Exploitation in the wild means attackers are actively using a vulnerability against real targets, not just testing it in a lab.
exploited in the wild concept
Exploited in the wild means attackers are actively using a vulnerability against real targets, not just in a lab.

Exploits are code or techniques that take advantage of software vulnerabilities.
Exposed concept
Accessible in a way that could allow a threat to reach or affect a system.
exposed identities concept
Exposed identities are user, service, or machine accounts whose credentials or access details may be visible to unauthorized people.

People outside an organization who are allowed to interact with its systems or communications.
also: external senders

An extortion-related threat-actor name referenced in security reporting.

A fallback is a backup option used when the preferred option is unavailable or fails.

The letters after a file name's final period that usually indicate its format, such as .pdf or .exe.

Financial accounts are accounts that hold or track money, credit, investments, or other financial assets.
financial assets concept
Financial assets are things with monetary value, such as cash, bank balances, stocks, bonds, or digital assets.
financial data concept
Financial data is information about money, accounts, payments, income, or transactions.

Fireside Consulting is an organization or company referenced in security reporting.
Fireside Consulting LLC organization
A consulting company referenced in security-related event or speaker information.
firewalls product

flaw concept
A flaw is a weakness or mistake in software, design, or configuration that can cause problems or security risk.

A method of using mathematics to prove that software or a system follows specified rules.
formula dragging concept
An Excel action that copies a formula into nearby cells by dragging the cell's fill handle.

Found is an organization referenced in security reporting.

Efforts to deceive people in order to steal money, information, or access.

geolocation concept

germany
Germany is a European country often referenced in cybersecurity reporting as a target, regulator, or law-enforcement partner.

Online platforms that connect workers with temporary, freelance, or task-based jobs.

A software component written in the Go programming language that performs tasks on a device.
Google organization
Google is a technology company that provides online services, including email-related services.

privileges concept

received@order[.]dell[.]com other

reconnaissance technique

redirect concept

remediation technique

remote access concept

remote control technique

A software component that an application downloads from an outside server when it runs instead of including directly in its published package.

Remote management tools let administrators control, monitor, or fix computers from another location, but attackers can also abuse them.
remote-code-execution technique

Remotely is a remote administration tool that can be used to access and manage computers over a network.
Replayed technique

repositories concept

repository concept
A repository is a storage location for code, files, and their change history, especially in systems like GitHub.
researchers organization
Researchers are people who study systems, threats, or vulnerabilities to understand and improve security.
Respond technique

Response decisions are choices an organization makes after discovering a security incident, such as containing it or notifying affected people.
Restore technique
Restore means to bring data, settings, or a system back to an earlier working state.

revocation path concept

rollback technique

root concept

root-level concept
Root-level means having the highest level of control over a device or operating system.
rotr technique

routers product

run code concept
To run code means to make a computer execute instructions written in a programming language.
runtime concept
Runtime is the period when a program is actively running, or the software environment it needs in order to run.
russia
Russia is a country frequently referenced in cybersecurity stories involving cybercrime groups, espionage, and government activity.
Russian targets concept
Russian targets are people, systems, facilities, or organizations in Russia selected for attention or attack.

safeguards concept
Safeguards are protections put in place to reduce the chance or impact of harm, misuse, or security incidents.
sanctions concept
Government-imposed restrictions that block or limit trade, financial dealings, or travel with targeted individuals or countries.
Saved Credentials concept
Saved credentials are passwords, tokens, or other login details stored by software for later use.

Saved passwords are login credentials stored by a browser, app, or password manager for later use.
scammers threat-actor

scams concept

scanner tool

scanning technique

scans concept

scope concept
scope defines what access, targets, or permissions are included in a security test, login request, or authorization grant.

screen recording technique

Security advisories concept

Security alerts concept

Security awareness concept

security checks technique

security control concept

security controls concept

security data concept

security patches concept

security policies concept

security products concept

security risks concept

security software product

security teams concept
Groups of professionals responsible for protecting an organization's information, systems, and networks from cyber threats.

Microsoft security patches released in September 2026.

sort-imports-es6-autofix product
